doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
title: How the soprano experiment ended, and flutes and clarinets
summary: The soprano idea lasted only a few tunes, and Mandel says flutes and clarinets were out of fashion but he used them for high sounds in The Song Is You.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So how did your experiments with Elliott go?
Oh, it was just something we did for a few tunes and then I dropped it and Tiny wrote some things and you know Al kinda laughed his way through it.

I don’t think he wrote anything for it but I kind of liked having the light sound for change, I was so sick of the tenors by then, you know the tenors were fine in the mid-40s and later 40s but everybody was tenor happy and I really didn’t like hearing the one alto hanging out there.
Yeah, its interesting Bill Russo in one of his composing/arranging books years ago made a statement, he said that, “one of the biggest lackings in the jazz orchestra is soprano instruments.”
That was before the soprano got really popular in the big-band writing, before…
You know the flutes hadn’t come in.
And it was real nice when Basie’s stuff, for instance, had the four flutes or three flutes and things like that.
And clarinets except for Ellington’s band were passé.
Passé, nobody wanted them, I used them, you could hear in, “The Song is You,” and things like that, I needed that.
Needed something that got up high, and from very early on I liked writing 5 and 6 ways, very much.
